headline: I gave ChatGPT my medical records. It was less scary—and more useful—than expected
summary: For obvious reasons, allowing ChatGPT to give medical advice is fraught with controversy. Is it really a good idea to trust a large language model with our health? Those are all good causes for concern, but they’re not stopping OpenAI from rolling out ChatGPT’s new health-oriented features to all U.S. users. First introduced earlier this year, ChatGPT Health can — with your permission — tap into a variety of medical data sources, ranging from telemetry from the Apple Health app to records from your doctor, and (as OpenAI carefully words it) help you “understand your information in context.” Now, it just so happens that hours before OpenAI announced its broader ChatGPT Health rollout, I had my annual physical. It was a routine visit (no major problems, phew!), and I’m lucky to have a general practitioner who’s friendly, down to earth, and clear about his findings. Among his directives: watch my diet, exercise more, and cut back on the cocktails. (Oh, c’mon, Doc!) Normally, I wouldn’t feel the need to feed my checkup details to an AI chatbot; generally speaking, I only like knowing what I need to know about my various health conditions. But this is PCWorld, and I cover AI for a living, so I took a deep breath and agreed to let ChatGPT check my chart. Just to be clear, right up front: This isn’t a full review, and I am in no way suggesting you try ChatGPT Health yourself unless you really want to. While the service uses a secure portal for linking medical records to ChatGPT and permissions controls abound, I believe there are still plenty of privacy concerns, and by no means should ChatGPT’s musings be confused with the diagnosis of a doctor (as OpenAI is quick to say). headline: Microsoft finally found a Windows ad it doesn’t like
summary: Microsoft is an advertising company. Not just an advertising company, true, it makes software and hardware and sells online services. But it made $10 billion in revenue from “search and news advertising” in 2025, according to its own numbers. This isn’t a new problem — despite being paid software, Windows is absolutely stuffed with advertising, stem to stern. But recently, some owners of LG monitors noticed that they were getting extra ads delivered via Windows Update, ostensibly disguised as helpful software. Not ads for Microsoft services. Not ads for LG products. Ads for McAfee, the kind of bloatware that’s been clogging up budget laptops with pre-installed junk since the 90s. They were, understandably, upset. Now Microsoft, of all companies, is doing damage control. LG monitors auto-install McAfee adware and popups via Windows Update Here’s how this is supposed to work. It’s the kind of thing that’s supposed to be invisible, doing the work behind the scenes so that you don’t really have to think about drivers or updates. headline: Two free apps every eBook reader should know about
summary: Today, you don’t even need to physically visit your local library to enjoy the books it offers. If you have a library card, there’s a good chance you can borrow eBooks, audiobooks, comics, movies, TV shows, and even music without ever walking into a branch. My two favorite apps for this are Libby and Hoopla, and they’re both completely free through participating libraries. Libby Libby is the app I recommend if you mostly want ebooks and audiobooks. It connects directly to your local library’s digital collection, so just about anything in print you’ll find in person will be available on this app. The catch is that popular titles often have waiting lists. If every copy is checked out, you’ll need to place a hold and wait your turn. The upside is that Libby usually offers a larger selection of bestselling books, magazines, and new releases. The app is clean, easy to use, and works across Android and Apple devices such as phones and tablets. It also supports most e-readers and web browsers. Hoopla Hoopla takes a slightly different approach. Instead of waiting in a digital queue, most titles are available instantly. Your library gives you a set number of monthly borrows, and you can use them on ebooks, audiobooks, movies, TV shows, comics, or music. Its catalog isn’t always as deep as Libby’s for new books, but the instant access is hard to beat. So if you decide you want to start an audiobook on your lunch break, chances are good you can begin listening right away. Fortunately, if your library supports both apps, there’s no reason to choose just one. I use Libby when I’m after a specific bestseller and Hoopla when I want something to read or watch without waiting. If you can’t get to the library, these apps are the next best thing—old book smell not included.
